catalog_locator: §2.4 声調 [Tone], p. 92, with §2.3.1 p. 89 on /ə/
catalog_quote: 2.4 声調 ウスイ語における声調としては（27）にしめす二種類をみとめる。(27) a. 中平調（M）: 無標、V でしめす: V33 ∼V22 程度で発音される。 b. 下降調（F）: 有標、V̀ でしめす: V31 ∼V21 程度で発音される。 /ə/は独自の声調をになわず、無声化するか軽声のように発音される。声門閉鎖音（ʔ）におわる音節はつねにややたかめのピッチで発音され、声調の区別はない。 最小対語・疑似最小対語の例を（28）にあげる。 (28) a. ka「サンダルを履く」vs. kà「のぼる」 ... なお、ウスイ語の個々の単語におけるピッチのあらわれは、実際には、初頭子音の有声性に依存するところがおおきい。すなわち、無声子音にはじまる音節のピッチは相対的にたかく、有声子音にはじまる音節のピッチは相対的にはひくくきこえる傾向にある。同様の傾向はバングラ語にもある。ピッチが実際にはどのようにあらわれるかについては、厳密にはまだわかっていない。 また、文中ではイントネーションがかぶさる結果、急激な下降やゆるやかな上昇が音声的にはきかれうる。傾向としては、文末の文法的小辞は急激な下降調で、文中における一音韻語の末尾、とくに従属節の末尾においては、上昇調で発音される。しかし、さらなる厳密な条件はまだあきらかではない。 [§2.3.1, p. 89] 母音のうち/ə/は単語の最終音節にはあらわれず、声調をになうこともない。
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: ウスイ語における声調としては（27）にしめす二種類をみとめる。(27) a. 中平調（M）: 無標、V でしめす: V33∼V22 程度で発音される。 b. 下降調（F）: 有標、V̀ でしめす: V31∼V21 程度で発音される。/ə/は独自の声調をになわず、無声化するか軽声のように発音される。声門閉鎖音（ʔ）におわる音節はつねにややたかめのピッチで発音され、声調の区別はない。[...] なお、ウスイ語の個々の単語におけるピッチのあらわれは、実際には、初頭子音の有声性に依存するところがおおきい。[p.89:] 母音のうち/ə/は単語の最終音節にはあらわれず、声調をになうこともない。
new_statements.translation: As tones in Usui we recognise the two kinds shown in (27): (27a) mid-level tone (M): unmarked, written V, pronounced at about 33~22; (27b) falling tone (F): marked, written V̀, pronounced at about 31~21. /ə/ does not carry a tone of its own; it is devoiced or pronounced like a neutral ('light') tone. Syllables ending in the glottal stop (ʔ) are always pronounced at a somewhat higher pitch and show no tonal contrast. [...] Moreover, the realisation of pitch in individual Usui words in fact depends largely on the voicing of the initial consonant. [p.89:] Among the vowels, /ə/ does not occur in the final syllable of a word and never bears tone.
new_statements.citation: Huziwara Keisuke [藤原敬介]. 2008. ウスイ語文法の概要 [An outline of Usui grammar]. 京都大学言語学研究 (Kyoto University Linguistic Research) 27: 81-124. doi:10.14989/73225

The '[..]' elides only the minimal pairs (28a-c). Surrounding section read: §2.1 syllable template C0əC1C2V1V2C3/T with C0ə- a minor syllable (fn.16: ə barely audible after voiceless C0), §2.4 continues wit…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Usui/Usoi is analysed as a two-tone language (mid-level vs falling) on full syllables; the schwa of prefixal minor syllables (C0ə-) is toneless and reduced/devoiced, and ʔ-checked syllables are toneless-high. The source gives no statement about word stress or accent placement; Brahma 2015 on Uchai likewise posits two tones (falling vs rising) and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: ʔ-final syllables carry no tone contrast (always somewhat high); /ə/ minor syllables toneless; pitch co-varies with onset voicing; sentence-final particles get sharp falls and clause-final words rises (intonation), per Huziwara 2008 p.92.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is lexical per (major) syllable; Huziwara 2009 fn.11 notes a possible word-tone tendency (one tone per phonological word) in compounds. No word- or phrase-level stress domain is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Huziwara (2008, 2009, 2011, 2012) describes Usoi as spoken in Bandarban / Karnaphuli basin, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh (one consultant from Roanchari). Brahma (2015) describes Uchai (Uchoi) of Tripura state, India. Glottolog files both under usui1238 'Usui'; both authors treat the variety as a southern Tripura/Kokborok lect close to Reang/Riang (rian1262) and distinct from Agartala Kokborok (kokb1239, described by Jacquesson 2008), so Kokborok stress statements should not be transferred to this key.

new_statements.quote: Kok Borok is a tonal language (Kokborok – Language of Borok people of Tripura). [...] Standard Kok Borok has tones, but whether all varieties of Kok Borok have tones is not clear. To the researchers Usoi Kau Brung sounded more tonal than the other varieties researched in Bangladesh, but whether the tones occur in minimal pairs is not known. [p. 64:] An exception might be the Rawangchari area, where Usoi speakers’ pronunciation and intonation may be noticeably different from the Usoi Kau Brung spoken in other parts of Bandarban.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Huziwara 2008 statement (tone language, two tones, no stress statement): the survey also treats the language as tonal and says nothing about stress, but it is weaker and impressionistic (no tone inventory for Usoi, minimal pairs 'not known'); the explicit low/high tone description it quotes is Jacquesson's on standard Kok Borok, not Usoi. It adds nothing to the catalog on stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement on word stress or accent anywhere in the 269 pages (the words 'stress' and 'accent' occur only in non-phonological senses, e.g. 'Barisal accent' of Bangla). The report is a sociolinguistic survey (wordlists, RTTs, questionnaires), not a phonology; it says Kok Borok is tonal (quoting Jacquesson 2003 on a low vs high tone contrast in standard/Debbarma Kok Borok) and that Usoi Kau Brung impressionistically 'sounded more tonal' than the other Bangladesh varieties, with minimal pairs unverified. The Appendix A wordlists carry no tone or stress diacritics.
new_statements.exceptions: none; only the remark that Rawangchari Usoi differs in 'pronunciation and intonation'
new_statements.identity_note: Kim et al. 2011 covers several Tripura varieties of Bangladesh: Usoi Tripura (Kau Brung, Bandarban district, incl. a Rawangchari sub-variety noted for different 'pronunciation and intonation'), Debbarma Kok Borok, Riang (Kau Bru), and ten Khagrachari Kok Borok groups. The only Usoi-specific prosodic remark is the impression that it 'sounded more tonal' than the other varieties; the low/high tone description quoted from Jacquesson (2003:110) is about standard Kok Borok, not Usoi. Huziwara's Usui (Usoi) data are from Bangladesh (Bandarban); Brahma 2015 describes Uchai of Tripura state, India.

tone_statements.quote: It also appears that the oldest speakers have a system different from that of Tripura in India and Bodo, among other BG languages, with a High tone, a Mid tone and a Falling tone. [...] Tone has almost disappeared among the speakers of Tripura in Bangladesh, especially young speakers, probably due to the influence of majority languages in Bangladesh like Bangla and Chakma (Huziwara 2003). [...] From the data, it appears that three tones exist in Tripura. The ‘High’ tone is somewhat rising, ‘Mid’ tone is mid slightly falling, and ‘Falling’ tone is indeed falling sharply from fairly high. [...] Mostly, one tone can occur per word.

sources.citation: Brahma, Tamojoy. 2011. Phonology of Uchai. Language in India 11(12) (December 2011): 402-426.
sources.quote: Uchai shows a two way tone contrast. The average pitch which is predominant in Uchai is toneless; on the contrary, the tone which is lower than the average might be termed as low or falling tone and that which is higher than the average as high or rising tone. [...] Uchai has two tones – low and high – which can occur with all the vowels, except mid central vowel /ə/. In single syllable words, the contrast between rising and falling tone is quite clear than the words with two or more syllables.
sources.locator: §6 Tone, p. 422, examples p. 423; §7 Conclusion, p. 425
sources.note: §6 Tone (pp.422-423) and §7 Conclusion (p.425): inventory '6 vowels, 5 diphthongs, 21 consonants and two tones'; two-way contrast low/falling vs high/rising against a predominant 'toneless' average pitch, five monosyllabic minimal pairs (rì 'give': rí 'draw a line', wà 'bite': wá 'hog'..); Kokborok final /k/ corresponds to Uchai diphthong or high tone (hik: hí 'wife'); tones occur on all vowels except /ə/; contrast clearer in monosyllables. Same count as the statement listed here (2) but characterised as low-falling vs high-rising rather than Huziwara's mid-level vs falling.
